⟦0⟧ can gain -3% consumer goods at ⟦1⟧ with its spirits, but will not gain additional factories by this.

Suppose the ⟦0⟧ is enabled and no other modifiers apply, meaning that the final consumer goods need is 30%. A country has 50 ⟦1⟧, 50 ⟦2⟧, and 20 ⟦3⟧. It will then have to allocate 30 ⟦4⟧ to produce consumer goods, leaving it with 15 that it can use freely.

Consumer Goods Factories factor (CGFF) is an additional factor that is available in some countries, most notably ⟦0⟧. It is the additional percentages of consumer goods in porportion to the current consumer goods factories. The number is multiplicative, not additive.
The following is the formula regarding CGFF:
Total Consumer Goods = Consumer Goods granted by Economy Law ⋅ ( 1 + CGFF ) {\displaystyle {\text{Total Consumer Goods}}={\text{Consumer Goods granted by Economy Law}}\cdot (1+{\text{CGFF}})}

Suppose a country with ⟦0⟧, meaning a consumer goods need of ⟦1⟧, and has ⟦2⟧ CGFF. It will have a final consumer goods need of 30% x (1+10%) = ⟦3⟧, not 40%. This means if it had 100 total factories, 33 civilian factories will be allocated to producing consumer goods.

In some cases CGFF can go into the negatives. Similar what happens with positive CGFF, this will reduce the current consumer goods need multiplicatively. If the same example country with ⟦0⟧ had ⟦1⟧ CGFF instead, its final consumer goods need would be 30% x (1-10%) = ⟦2⟧, not 20%.

Multiple sources of CGFF stack multiplicatively with each other. This means that multiple smaller sources of positive CGFF can have a greater effect than a single, larger source of positive CGFF. Inversely, a single large source of negative CGFF will have a greater effect than multiple smaller sources of negative CGFF.

There are also modifiers which only affect a single type of building. These are, primarily, the ⟦0⟧ (Captain of Industry, Fortification Engineer, Quartermaster General and War Industrialist) but can also be one of many other ⟦1⟧ activated by ⟦2⟧ or ⟦3⟧.

The return on investment of building an additional Civilian Factory will depend on the ⟦0⟧ bonus as well the Economy Law currently in place, or expected in the future. The higher the Construction Speed bonus is, the more Output will be done by the newly built Civilian Factory and the faster it will accumulate an Output equal to its cost, 10800. This variable is the time, in days, required to recover the cost of building the factory, or payback time.

A country's ⟦0⟧ will, in addition to sometimes affecting civilian factory construction speed, also dictate what ratio of civilian factories are used for fulfilling consumer goods needs vs. for free use as output, ⟦1⟧, etc. The higher this ratio is, the longer the payback time of newly built civilian factories will be, as there is a greater likelihood that a newly built civilian factory will be allocated to producing consumer goods instead of having useful output. The payback time of a new civilian factory is given by the following formula:

Construction speed modifiers range between ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧. Except for the lowest two modifiers, they all have multiple combinations to be achieved. In fact, there are 320 possible combinations of variables affecting civilian factory construction speed outside of national spirits and unique laws. The infrastructure bonus ranges from ⟦2⟧ at zero infrastructure to ⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ at max infrastructure.

For example, at 3/5 infrastructure in a state, construction speed in that state is multiplied by ⟦0⟧. In the Construction UI, this bonus is displayed for each State as a colored percentage next to an Infrastructure road icon. This bonus is applied after bonuses from tech, advisors, and national spirits, making 1 level of infrastructure a more powerful bonus than, e.g., a War Industrialist.

It is usually recommended to allocate an infrastructure/civilian factory building phase for your nation before subsequently militarizing by building military factories and naval dockyards. However, the scope of civilian factory building can be reduced substantially if early warfare is planned or expected, and/or if newly built dockyards are meant to produce ships with very long production times.

Due to the construction boost from infrastructure, the most efficient method involves filling all building slots one state at a time. This can be done by prioritizing states with higher starting infrastructure levels. The mechanics of the game encourages players to concentrate industry in central, high-infrastructure areas, although this must be balanced against the increased vulnerability of having all of one's industry in one place. It is common for all building slots to be filled before the game ends, this represents the in-game factory cap for the respective territory.

Anti-air provides damage resistance from bomber-type attacks (port strikes and strategic bombing) depending on the level of anti-air in the containing state and researched anti-air technologies. Dispersed Industry provides an alternative source of damage resistance but only for factories and not stacking with anti-air. The maximum of the two is used for factories.
